terms.meaning: a shared frame that wraps every page so common parts appear everywhere
a wrapper component that gives the pages inside it shared settings, such as the theme or the data loader
the settings that control how a page scales on a phone or tablet screen
the step where the browser attaches interactivity to a page that the server already drew
a web app that can be installed on a phone and used like a native app

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and fonts
sections.what: Brings in the shared pieces the app needs and loads two fonts, Inter and Outfit, so text can use them. This section does not appear on screen by itself.
sections.why: Fonts and providers must be loaded once here so every page can use them.

sections.name: metadata
sections.title: Page title and app icon data
sections.what: Sets the browser tab title, the short description, the web app manifest link, and the title used when the app is saved to an iPhone home screen.
sections.why: Makes the app show a proper name and description in browsers and when installed.

sections.name: viewport
sections.title: Mobile screen scaling rules
sections.what: Tells phones to fit the page to the screen width and blocks zooming in or out. It also sets the browser bar color to a purple shade.
sections.why: Keeps the layout stable on small screens, though the reason for blocking zoom is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Blocking zoom prevents people with low vision from enlarging text, so this setting should be reviewed.

sections.name: RootLayout
sections.title: Overall page frame and providers
sections.what: Builds the outer html and body tags, sets the language to English, and applies the font classes. It wraps the page content with the data provider and theme provider, then adds the install prompt, offline notice, toast messages, and analytics.
sections.why: Puts every shared feature in one place so each page gets them automatically.
sections.watch_out: The theme provider is set to follow the system setting by default, so the app may look different from what the designer expects on some devices.

summary: The outer frame of every page in the web app, which sets the fonts, the page title, the mobile view settings, and the shared providers.
purpose: Wraps every page so they share the same fonts, theme switching, data loading setup, notifications, and analytics.
why: Next.js uses this single layout file as the entry point for the whole app, so shared setup belongs here.
how: It loads two Google fonts and sets the page title, description, and app icon data. It sets mobile viewport rules, then renders the html and body tags. Inside the body, it wraps the page content with the data provider and the theme provider, and adds the install prompt, offline notice, toast messages, and analytics.
inputs: The page content passed in as children, plus the theme and data settings defined in the providers.
outputs: The complete HTML frame for every page, with fonts and shared components already in place.
risks: The viewport settings block pinch zoom, which is an accessibility problem for users with low vision. The analytics import sits in the middle of the file, which is easy to miss when editing.
debug: If every page looks unstyled, check the font loading and that globals.css is imported. If theme switching does not work, check the theme provider settings. If the page cannot zoom on a phone, check the viewport block first.
